teaching.causalExplanation: The method is simple. Be greedy, but careful. List the links from cheapest to dearest. Then take them one at a time. If a link joins something new, keep it. If it would close a loop, a cycle, skip it, because everything it joins is already connected. Stop when every tower is connected, which for five towers is after four links. Why does this work? Every link we keep is the cheapest way left to bring in something new. And skipping a link that closes a cycle never disconnects anything, because those towers are already joined. This is called Kruskal's method, but you don't need the name. You need the steps. Cheapest first, skip any cycle, and stop when it spans. Let's run it. In order, the links are two, three, four, five, six, seven and eight. C to D, two. Nothing's connected yet, so keep it. A to C, three. A is new, so keep it. D to E, four. E is new, keep it. B to C, five. B is new, keep it. That's four links, and all five towers are connected, so we could stop. But watch what the rest would do. C to E, six, would close the loop C, D, E, so skip it. B to D, seven, closes B, C, D. Skip. And A to B, eight, closes A, B, C. Skip. The minimum spanning tree is C D, A C, D E and B C, for a total of fourteen kilometres. Check with the count. Five towers, four links, no loops, and every tower joined. That's a spanning tree, and nothing cheaper can do the job. That's the answer to a minimal connector problem. Connect everything, with the least total length. Fourteen kilometres instead of thirty-five. At twenty-five thousand dollars a kilometre, that's three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, instead of eight hundred and seventy-five thousand. And every tower can still reach every other, through the tree. Councils use the same idea for water mains, farms for irrigation pipes, and power companies for lines to new houses. Whenever a question says connect them all as cheaply as possible, it's a minimal connector problem, and a minimum spanning tree answers it.
